chapters.title: Chapter 1: The Idea of Pairs Trading

lessons.title: Long-Short Construction: Building a Market-Neutral Position

children.text: A new pairs trader decides to go long 100 shares of HDFC Bank and short 100 shares of ICICI Bank, treating "100 shares on each side" as balanced. It is not. If HDFC Bank trades near ₹1,650 and ICICI Bank near ₹1,200 (illustrative levels), the long leg is worth roughly ₹1.65 lakh while the short leg is worth only ₹1.2 lakh. That extra ₹45,000 of unhedged long exposure means a chunk of the position is quietly a directional bet on the market, not a market-neutral pairs trade at all. Getting the sizing right, not just picking the right pair, is what actually makes a trade market neutral.

body.text: A market-neutral position is built rupee for rupee, not share for share. The long leg and the short leg need roughly equal rupee value, using a hedge ratio to convert between the two stocks' different prices, so that a broad market move affects both legs by a similar rupee amount and mostly cancels out.

markDefs.definition: The ratio used to convert between two stocks' different prices so that the long and short legs of a pairs trade carry roughly equal rupee exposure.

children.text: The simplest way to size a pair is to match rupee value on each leg using a

: the price of the long stock divided by the price of the short stock. This tells you how many shares of the short stock to trade for every share of the long stock, so both legs end up worth roughly the same in rupees. This naive, price-ratio hedge ratio is a reasonable starting point. Chapter 2 builds a more precise, regression-based hedge ratio that accounts for how much each stock actually moves relative to the other, not just their price levels, but the rupee-neutral logic underneath both approaches is identical.

body.caption: Naive price-ratio hedge ratio: shares to short per share held long, so both legs carry equal rupee value

children.text: A Worked Example: Sizing the HDFC Bank / ICICI Bank Pair

Say you want to deploy ₹5 lakh on the long leg, HDFC Bank at ₹1,650, and an equal ₹5 lakh on the short leg, ICICI Bank at ₹1,200. The number of HDFC Bank shares is ₹5,00,000 divided by ₹1,650, which is about 303 shares. Using the hedge ratio, 1,650 divided by 1,200 equals 1.375, so for every HDFC Bank share held long you short 1.375 ICICI Bank shares. That gives 303 multiplied by 1.375, or about 417 ICICI Bank shares to short. Check the rupee values: 303 shares of HDFC Bank at ₹1,650 is close to ₹5,00,000, and 417 shares of ICICI Bank at ₹1,200 is close to ₹5,00,400. The two legs are now balanced in rupee terms, not in share count.

body.text: Notice the share counts are quite different, 303 versus 417, even though the rupee exposure on each leg is nearly identical. This is exactly why matching share counts, as in the opening example, leaves a position unintentionally unbalanced.

children.text: Two Ways to Get Short in the Indian Market

Buying the long leg is straightforward: place a delivery order through your broker, like Zerodha, and the shares sit in your demat account. Shorting is where Indian market structure adds a real constraint. SEBI rules do not allow retail investors to carry a naked short position in cash equities overnight. A short sale in the cash market must be squared off intraday unless the position is covered through NSE's Securities Lending and Borrowing (SLB) mechanism, where you formally borrow the shares you are shorting for a fee and a fixed tenure. In practice, most pairs traders holding a position for more than a day use the short leg in stock futures instead of cash shares. Shorting a futures contract needs no borrowing arrangement, can be held for weeks, and is the standard route prop desks and systematizing retail traders use to build multi-day pairs positions.

points: You short the exact stock at the exact price you choose
Requires locating a lender and paying a borrowing fee, availability varies by stock
Position must be returned at the end of the SLB contract tenure
No expiry-driven rollover needed while the borrow is active

columns.label: Short via stock futures
points: No borrowing needed, short a futures contract like any other order
Can only trade in fixed lot sizes, not arbitrary share counts
Position must be rolled over to the next series before monthly expiry
Requires SPAN plus exposure margin, and moves with mark-to-market daily

body.text: Stock futures trade in fixed lot sizes set by NSE, not single shares. If ICICI Bank's lot size is, say, 700 shares, you cannot short exactly 417 shares through futures, you can only short in multiples of 700. This rounding, along with the margin and mark-to-market mechanics of futures, is exactly why real-world hedge ratios are rarely perfect and need periodic rebalancing, a practical constraint Chapter 4 covers when sizing and managing a live pair.

children.text: Where This Naive Ratio Falls Short

The price-ratio hedge ratio used above only accounts for the two stocks' current prices. It says nothing about how much each stock actually tends to move relative to the other. If ICICI Bank has historically moved 1.2 rupees for every 1 rupee move in HDFC Bank, a purely price-based hedge ratio ignores that entirely, and the position will not be as market neutral as it looks on paper. Chapter 2 replaces this naive ratio with one estimated from a regression between the two stocks' actual price histories, which is the version used to build a proper spread and z-score signal.

body.label: NSE F&O lot size and contract specifications
body.description: Check current lot sizes and margin requirements before sizing a stock futures leg of a pairs trade.

body.title: Calculate the hedge ratio shares
body.prompt: You are long 500 shares of Britannia Industries at ₹4,800 and want to short Nestle India at ₹2,400 to build a rupee-neutral pair. Using the price-ratio hedge ratio, how many Nestle India shares should you short?
body.explanation: Hedge ratio h = 4,800 / 2,400 = 2. Shares to short = h × 500 = 1,000 shares. Check: 500 × ₹4,800 = ₹24,00,000 long, and 1,000 × ₹2,400 = ₹24,00,000 short, so both legs carry equal rupee value.

body.title: The lot size problem
body.scenario: Your calculated hedge ratio says you need to short 417 shares of ICICI Bank, but ICICI Bank's futures lot size is 700 shares, and you do not have access to SLB for this stock.
body.prompt: What are your realistic options, and what trade-off does each one involve?
body.modelAnswer: You could short one full lot (700 shares) via futures, which overhedges the position beyond your calculated ratio and leaves you net short the relationship rather than neutral. You could scale up the long leg (more HDFC Bank shares) so that 700 ICICI Bank shares is the correct hedge ratio, which increases your total capital deployed and risk. Or you could look for a different candidate pair where the lot size divides more cleanly into your target position size. Each option trades off precision, capital use, or pair selection, there is no way to short exactly 417 shares through the futures route.

cards.definition: The ratio used to convert between two stocks' prices so the long and short legs of a pairs trade carry roughly equal rupee exposure.
A position where the long and short legs are sized to have roughly equal rupee value, as opposed to an equal number of shares.
NSE's mechanism for formally borrowing shares for a fee and a fixed tenure, used to hold a short cash equity position beyond a single trading day.
The fixed minimum quantity in which a stock futures or options contract must be traded, set by the exchange and different for each underlying stock.
The exchange-mandated margin, calculated using the Standard Portfolio Analysis of Risk methodology, required to hold a futures position, adjusted daily with mark-to-market.

points: A market-neutral position is sized rupee for rupee using a hedge ratio, not share for share, because two stocks rarely trade at similar prices.
The naive price-ratio hedge ratio (long price divided by short price) is a reasonable starting point, refined into a regression-based hedge ratio in Chapter 2.
Indian cash equity short sales must be squared off intraday unless covered through NSE's Securities Lending and Borrowing (SLB) mechanism.
Most multi-day pairs trades short the futures leg instead, avoiding the need to borrow shares, at the cost of fixed lot sizes, expiry-driven rollovers, and SPAN plus exposure margin.
Lot size rounding means a calculated hedge ratio can rarely be matched exactly through futures, which is why real pairs positions need periodic rebalancing.
Sizing correctly is what actually makes a trade market neutral. An unbalanced position quietly becomes a directional bet, no matter how well the pair itself was chosen.
